title: I Put My House in a Trust to Protect It From Nursing Home Costs. The Timing Almost Ruined It.
summary: The timing of a trust transfer can decide whether your home is protected from nursing home costs. Here are the rules.
body_markdown:
An irrevocable trust may help protect your property when you need Medicaid to pay for nursing home care. Transferring assets too late, however, could delay coverage for months or even years. Here are the rules that could affect your ability to pay for care and keep your home. Knowing them ahead of time could prevent a transfer penalty that delays coverage.


## How Nursing Home Costs Could Put Your Home at Risk


For many retirees, a home is the largest asset they own, and long-term care can drain their savings. Medicare pays for limited skilled nursing care, usually after a qualifying hospital stay.1 It doesn’t[cover custodial care](https://smartasset.com/retirement/custodial-care) , such as help with bathing, dressing and eating, when that’s all you need.2


Medicaid covers long-term custodial care for people who meet state income and asset limits. A primary residence may be excluded, depending on who lives there, its equity and other eligibility rules.3 The home can still be claimed through Medicaid estate recovery after the recipient dies, subject to federal and state protections and exceptions.4


The table shows how each source of payment treats long-term care and what it could mean for your home:


Payment Source What It Covers Limits Risk to Your Home


[Medicare](https://smartasset.com/insurance/medicare-eligibility) Short-term skilled nursing care after a qualifying hospital stay Up to 100 days per benefit period; no custodial care Doesn’t pay for long stays, so savings or the home may be needed


[Medicaid](https://smartasset.com/insurance/who-qualifies-for-medicaid) Long-term custodial care in a nursing facility Strict income and asset limits that vary by state Home may be excluded during your lifetime but subject to estate recovery


[Long-term care insurance](https://smartasset.com/insurance/best-long-term-care-insurance) Care costs up to the policy’s daily or lifetime limits Premiums, waiting periods and benefit caps Can reduce the need to tap home equity


[Personal savings](https://smartasset.com/checking-account/savings-calculator) and[home equity](https://smartasset.com/mortgage/what-is-home-equity) Any type of care Limited by what you’ve saved The home may need to be sold once other savings run out


**A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_trusts&utm_content=puthouseintrusttoprotectitfromnursinghomecoststimingalmostruinedit_a) can help you estimate long-term care costs and decide how to pay for them without selling your home.**


## Why Timing Matters


Federal law applies a[60-month look-back period](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/medicaid-look-back-period) to certain asset transfers made before an application for long-term care coverage.5 A transfer during that period can trigger a penalty if Medicaid treats it as a gift or a sale for less than[fair market value](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/fair-market-value) .


Once the transfer falls outside the look-back period, it generally does not create a[transfer penalty](https://smartasset.com/retirement/how-to-avoid-medicaid-5-year-lookback) . Reaching the five-year mark does not fix trust terms that still give you access to the property or proceeds, so both timing and the terms of the trust matter.


Timing can protect your home only if you’ve also chosen the right kind of trust. A[revocable living trust](https://smartasset.com/retirement/what-is-a-revocable-living-trust) lets you change its terms or take a home back at any time, so Medicaid could count it toward the asset limit and put you over the financial threshold for coverage. An[irrevocable trust](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/irrevocable-trust) , by comparison, can protect your home if you give up access to the property and any sale proceeds. The table compares both:


Key Difference Revocable Living Trust Irrevocable Trust for Medicaid Planning


Control You can change or revoke the trust Your control is limited by the trust terms


Access to the property You keep access to the home and other trust assets Access to the property and principal is restricted


Medicaid eligibility Assets generally remain available, but transfers from the trust can still be subject to the look-back rules Property kept beyond your reach can be treated as unavailable


Five-year look-back Doesn’t apply, since Medicaid already counts the assets A transfer during the look-back period can trigger a penalty


Sale of the home You control the sale and proceeds The trustee handles a permitted sale, and proceeds remain subject to the trust


Living in the home You can continue living there Continued occupancy depends on the trust terms and state rules

## How to Avoid the Medicaid Timing Penalty


If you move your house into an irrevocable trust during the look-back period, Medicaid may calculate a penalty, dividing the home’s uncompensated value by your state’s average monthly cost of private nursing home care.6 That figure is the number of months Medicaid won’t pay for your[long-term care](https://smartasset.com/insurance/cost-of-long-term-care-insurance-at-age-60) , even if you otherwise qualify.


For example, a 70-year-old places a mortgage-free property worth $450,000 in the trust and applies three years later. Assuming the entire transfer is penalized, in a state where private care averages $10,000 a month, Medicaid would withhold benefits for 45 months ($450,000 ÷ $10,000). That clock starts only once the applicant needs facility-level support and meets every other eligibility rule, so the family would have to find another way to pay for care during those 45 months.


To avoid the penalty, fund the trust at least five years before you’re likely to require nursing home care. It must also meet Medicaid rules governing your access to the assets. Keeping long-term care insurance or savings available can pay those bills if that need arrives sooner. A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_trusts&utm_content=puthouseintrusttoprotectitfromnursinghomecoststimingalmostruinedit_a) may help you time the transfer and plan how to cover expenses during the look-back period.
